directions: Site this vigorous University of Minnesota selection where its glowing cherry-red-to-orange winter bark can be seen against snow or a dark backdrop, ideally in moist, slightly acidic soil near a pond edge or low spot. Water regularly during the first two seasons and mulch to keep roots cool, since the shrub is happiest with consistent moisture. Each late winter or very early spring, cut one-third of the oldest, dullest-colored canes to the ground so a steady supply of young stems carries the brightest color the following winter. Left unpruned it grows into a large, twiggy thicket, so give it room or plan on periodic hard renewal cuts.

This naturally compact sport, discovered near Isanti County, Minnesota, fits foundation plantings and smaller borders where full-size red-twig dogwoods would sprawl too far. Give it consistently moist soil and full sun for the deepest red winter bark and best fall foliage color. Because it suckers less aggressively than the species, an annual light shearing is optional, but for the strongest stem color remove about a quarter of the oldest wood at the base every year or two in late winter. It tolerates wet, poorly drained spots as well as average garden soil, making it useful along rain gardens or drainage swales.
sources: Iowa State University Extension and Outreach

directions: Bailey's dogwood forms an upright, rounded mass of deep red winter stems and spreads by layering rather than the wide-running underground stolons typical of the species, so it stays a bit more contained in a mixed shrub border. It adapts to both moist lowlands and average upland soil, and tolerates heavy clay better than many named selections. Prune out roughly a third of the oldest canes at ground level each late winter to keep replacing dull gray-brown wood with vivid young red growth, and expect to renew the whole clump on a hard three-to-four-year rotation if it becomes crowded. Full sun brings out the richest stem color, though it will still perform in light shade with somewhat duller bark.

Marketed under the Arctic Fire trademark, this dwarf, non-suckering selection delivers the same brilliant cherry-red winter stems as full-size red-twig dogwoods on a plant compact enough for a foundation planting or small-space rain garden. It thrives in consistently moist to wet soil but adapts to normal garden conditions with regular watering. Because it is far less prone to spreading by root suckers than the species, maintenance pruning can be lighter, but for peak stem brightness still cut one-quarter to one-third of the oldest stems to the ground in late winter every year or two. Plant in full sun for the strongest color; stems fade to green-brown with age regardless of light, which is why the renewal cuts matter.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

common_name: Silver and Gold Variegated Yellow-Twig Dogwood
directions: A sport of the yellow-stemmed 'Flaviramea', this cultivar layers creamy white leaf margins over the green summer foliage before revealing bright yellow-green winter bark once leaves drop, giving it two seasons of interest instead of one. Grow it in moist, humus-rich soil in full sun to light shade; some afternoon shade helps prevent leaf scorch on the variegated margins in hot climates. Remove about a third of the oldest, most faded stems at ground level in late winter each year so the shrub keeps producing the youngest wood, which carries the clearest gold color. Watch for occasional all-green reversion shoots and prune these out promptly so they do not overtake the variegated growth.

This compact, naturally rounded sport of 'Elegantissima' stays smaller and denser, making it easier to fit into mixed borders while still offering crisp white-margined foliage all summer and bright coral-red stems once the leaves drop. Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade, giving it afternoon shade in hot regions to keep the variegated leaves from scorching. Cut a third of the oldest stems to the ground in late winter each year to keep the plant supplied with the youngest wood, which shows the most vivid red bark, and shear out any solid-green reversion shoots as soon as you spot them. It tolerates both moist lowland sites and average garden soil once established.

This golden-leaved selection pairs soft chartreuse-to-yellow summer foliage with the coral-red winter stems typical of Tatarian dogwood, giving strong color from spring through winter. Grow it in part shade in hot climates to prevent leaf scorch, or full sun in cooler regions where the foliage color develops best without burning. It appreciates consistently moist, fertile soil but tolerates average garden conditions once established. Cut roughly one-third of the oldest canes down to the ground every late winter so the shrub continually renews itself with young stems, which hold both the brightest bark color and the most vibrant leaf color the following season.

Grown for its unusual near-black, purplish stems that create a striking contrast against snow, this selection also carries purple-tinged summer foliage and turns reddish-purple in fall for an unusually dark, moody effect in the winter garden. Plant in moist, fertile soil in full sun for the darkest stem color and best foliage tint, though it tolerates part shade with somewhat less intensity. As with other Tatarian dogwoods, cut out about a third of the oldest stems at ground level each late winter, since the darkest, richest color is carried on one- and two-year-old wood and older stems fade to dull brown-gray. It combines well with white-stemmed birches or evergreens that show off the dark bark by contrast.

This standout bloodtwig dogwood produces a fiery blend of yellow, orange, and red on the same stems once the leaves drop, glowing most intensely when backlit by low winter sun. Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun, since stem color is noticeably more muted in shade, and water regularly through the first year or two while roots establish. For the strongest color display, cut the entire plant back hard to a low framework, or remove the oldest one-third of stems, every year or two in late winter just before new growth starts, because the multicolor effect is strongest on young, vigorous wood and fades to brown as stems age. It combines beautifully with evergreens or ornamental grasses that provide a backdrop for its winter color.
